coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean four-part argument: allocation effect, exit cost, customer evidence, plan. Their executive summaries map directly onto the slide titles. X is tight, but its headline exit figures are the no-migration case ($5.5M / $3.4M) while the governing thought gives a range and the best case sits in sub-points, so the reader must reconcile two sets of numbers. Its options table also says bundle fill 'stays at 91%' only under retain-unchanged, although the fill fix is independent of the redesign. Y uses one consistent pair ($4.75M / $2.65M at the migration ceiling, $3.4M before migration) throughout. Its governing thought names all three planks (redesign, bundle service, evidence-based sunset), and each is carried by a section, a gate and a board decision. Y's hypothesis-test slide and appendix add length but stay subordinate to the main line.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (retain C, redesign, fix bundle fill, revisit a 2029 sunset) and both reject immediate exit on contribution, penalties and constraints. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It compares four options on time-phased 2027–29 cash and against each board constraint. It shows no migration rate rescues exit (full migration still loses $0.4M a year). It stress-tests the redesign with a downside case and break-even thresholds, and tests price pressure (exit breaks even only if C contribution falls about 70%). Y also sets explicit gates: Gate 1 at a $0.4M run-rate saving, and Gate 2 with named criteria for a sunset. Y answers the 'redeploy to D' half of the question directly: sequence the team, and note that D's spare capacity is available whether or not C exits. It also covers the other seven bundle customers and pre-notification of the design change. X's judgment is sound: pilot-gated redesign, 2029 exit terms in renewals, a 2028 sunset review, and unknowns with owners. But its gates are qualitative and its options table is thinner; it leaves the engineering trade-off unquantified, which is what the pack asked for.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: $3.8M contribution, $0.4M avoidable, −$2.65M and −$4.75M at the migration ceiling, the $6.8M D break-even, and the 2.3x penalty-to-cash ratio. Neither treats the renewal gap as causal, and both expose the dashboard definition. X's arithmetic is correct (51% of shared cost on 18% of sales, 44% payback threshold, 5.3 months). It treats the penalty as counting against the $0.9M cash limit without flagging that as an assumption. Y's much larger set of calculations checks out: operating profit 10.1 → 7.45 / 6.7, the pro-rata reallocation margins, calendar-phased −3.43 / −8.7 / −10.6, redesign +2.37 base and +0.40 downside, 19% / 31% break-evens, 29% post-redesign margin, and the 70% price-pressure threshold. Y logs every calculation and assumption, including the penalty-in-envelope assumption and the invented timings. Y has two weaknesses. Its $0.25M 'illustrative ceiling' on engineering opportunity cost is not a true upper bound, since D work could expand capacity, and it sits close to what the pack warned against, though it is labelled as a bound and not an estimate. It also states the bundle shortfall is 'caused by A and B' slightly more firmly than the pack does. These are minor against Y's wider and more transparent use of the evidence.

revision.reasons: Both firmly reject the CEO's 'drop C on 8% margin' hypothesis, as the key expects. Both dismantle each supporting argument (allocated margin, D substitution, renewal correlation) and both keep the renewal question open instead of over-claiming ('neither proves nor rules out'). X addresses the CEO's case directly in a dedicated section and proposes like-for-like tests. Y goes further on the CEO's own logic. It shows that after exit the same margin ranking would make B the next 'weakest' while total allocated cost falls only $0.4M, and that the redesign would lift C's reported margin to about 29%. It also makes a causal renewal test an explicit sunset-gate criterion. Y's hypothesis-test slide is explicit about what holds, what is unproven and what needed refining (retain-as-is fails), but it frames the 'initial hypothesis' as the team's own 'keep C' rather than the CEO's, which is a little off-target. Net, Y's handling is somewhat more thorough.

overall.reasons: Both documents are defensible and meet all four of the key's criteria: margins reconciled to avoidable cash, the penalty treated as one-time, D substitution bounded by capacity and validation, and no causal reading of the renewal gap. Y serves the board better because it delivers more of what the committee asked for. It gives a time-phased comparison of exit, retain, delayed sunset and redesign against each constraint. It adds sensitivities showing the conclusion is robust: no migration rate makes exit pay, the redesign breaks even at 19–31% of the estimated saving, and exit needs a 70% fall in C contribution. It also provides a concrete contract plan, quantified gates and a transparent assumption log. X is accurate, leaner, and more disciplined about not quantifying the engineering opportunity cost. But it offers less decision support on downside cases, gate thresholds and the redeploy-to-D question.
